arc_intro:
FQ-203 — Deepak Menon (DevOps Lead)

Last thing for this ticket. Alarms and audit trail are solid now — but I want a single pane of glass where I can look at order-service's health at a glance without digging through individual metric graphs. And I've heard X-Ray mentioned as a way to trace slow requests — if that's what it is, I want to understand whether it actually adds anything we don't already have.

Oh, and before you build anything new — there's apparently already a CloudWatch dashboard for order-service that someone put together. Check what it's actually showing before we decide what to add.

— Deepak

Pull Trusted Advisor, Config, encryption, EBS, and S3 findings into one readiness pass.
arc_outro:
Deepak Menon (DevOps Lead)

That's exactly the kind of thing that gives people false confidence — a dashboard with a line going up and to the right that turns out to be measuring the number of data collection points, not actual requests. Easy mistake to make, genuinely hard to spot if you don't know what to look for.

Dashboard is correct now, X-Ray is showing us where the time actually goes in a real request. That's FQ-203 done. We went from finding out about outages from Twitter to having correct metrics, working alarms with proper notification paths, a full audit trail, and actual request tracing. Not bad for one ticket.

Next one's yours, Ravi.

— Deepak

tasks.question: Before trusting this graph as accurate, what should you check first?

B) Which specific metric STATISTIC the graph is using — the same underlying metric can look completely different depending on whether you're plotting Sum, Average, SampleCount, or a percentile, and a rising line does not by itself confirm the graph is measuring what its title claims
C) Whether the dashboard was built by a senior engineer, since seniority determines whether the graph is trustworthy
D) Whether the graph is using a line chart or a bar chart, since that determines the accuracy of the underlying data

tasks.question: For a metric like 'number of HTTP requests processed by order-service,' what's the difference between the SUM and SAMPLECOUNT statistics in CloudWatch?
options: A) They're identical — SUM and SAMPLECOUNT produce the same value for any metric

B) SUM adds up the actual metric VALUES in a period (for a request count metric, this gives you the total number of requests). SAMPLECOUNT counts how many DATA POINTS were reported to CloudWatch in that period — which is the number of metric observations, not the count of requests. If CloudWatch receives 3 data points reporting 120, 145, and 98 requests respectively, SUM = 363 (total requests), SAMPLECOUNT = 3 (three data points were reported)
C) SAMPLECOUNT always gives a larger number than SUM, making it better for dashboards that should look impressive
D) SUM is only available for billing metrics, not for application or infrastructure metrics
tasks.explanation: This exact distinction — SUM metric VALUES add does (real request count), SAMPLECOUNT data points's count (how many times CloudWatch received a measurement). Request volume for dashboard SUM is needed, SAMPLECOUNT-a kept, reporting frequency kaatudhu, actual traffic not.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — SUM actual values, SAMPLECOUNT measurement count. Request for volume SUM.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — SUM um SAMPLECOUNT um different different topic. SUM values add does, SAMPLECOUNT observations count does.

tasks.question: What does AWS X-Ray specifically add that CloudWatch metrics alone cannot provide?
options: A) X-Ray is simply a more expensive, redundant version of CloudWatch with no unique capability

B) X-Ray traces individual requests end-to-end THROUGH your application, showing exactly where time is spent at each step — which service call, which database query, which downstream API — as a connected trace. CloudWatch metrics tell you THAT latency is high at an aggregate level; X-Ray shows you exactly WHERE in the request that time is being spent and WHY
C) X-Ray provides real-time alerts, while CloudWatch only provides delayed metrics
D) X-Ray only works for Lambda functions, never for EC2 or containerized applications
tasks.explanation: X-Ray oda real value: individual request trace, end-to-end, each in step time breakdown. CloudWatch aggregate-a 'latency is high' kaatudhu, X-Ray specific-a 'this DB query took 800ms, this downstream API took 300ms' kaatudhu. Different different for questions answers, complementary tools.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — CloudWatch THAT something is slow, X-Ray WHERE and WHY, complementary not redundant.
tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — X-Ray CloudWatch redundant not. CloudWatch aggregate metrics, X-Ray individual request traces. Different different questions.

tasks.scenario: karthik-dev is adding a new widget showing 'Average Order Checkout Time' to the dashboard. He asks whether he should use SUM or AVERAGE for this metric.
tasks.question: Which statistic is correct for showing a typical checkout experience duration?
options: A) SUM — adding all checkout durations together gives the total time spent across all checkouts

B) AVERAGE — since the goal is to understand a typical user's experience, averaging the duration across all checkouts in a period gives a meaningful single number representing a representative checkout time; SUM would give a nonsensical 'total seconds spent checking out' figure that grows with traffic volume regardless of whether checkout speed actually changed
C) SAMPLECOUNT — counting the number of checkout events tells you the typical duration
D) SUM and AVERAGE are identical for duration metrics, so either works

SUM for duration use did, traffic high but SUM increase will happen duration actually faster-a even if, misleading-a will be. This T2's SUM-vs-SAMPLECOUNT lesson's complement — correct statistic, correct metric for type.

tasks.scenario: ananya-analyst reports that the CloudWatch average latency dashboard metric has been around 320ms for the past week, which seems acceptable. But some customers are still occasionally complaining about slow checkout. Deepak asks: 'What's a better metric to find the slow tail of requests, rather than the average?'
tasks.question: What statistic would reveal slow requests that the average hides?
options: A) SUM — adding all latency values would reveal the slow requests

B) A high-percentile statistic like p99 or p95 — these show the latency at which 99% or 95% of requests complete, exposing the slow tail that average hides. If average is 320ms but p99 is 4,200ms, it means 1% of requests take over 4 seconds — painful for those customers, completely invisible in the average
C) SAMPLECOUNT — counting the number of latency measurements reveals which ones are slow
D) MIN — finding the fastest request reveals what slow requests are being compared against

tasks.scenario: X-Ray is enabled on order-service. A customer reports their checkout took 8 seconds. The CloudWatch average latency metric shows nothing unusual (still around 320ms average). You pull the X-Ray trace for the specific slow request.
tasks.error_shown:
X-Ray Trace: Request ID fa3b2c1d-e9f8-4a7b-8c6d-5e4f3a2b1c0d
Total duration: 8,241ms
├── order-service handler: 142ms
├── → RDS query (get_user_cart): 7,803ms ← anomaly
├── → Razorpay API call (initiate_payment): 187ms
└── → order-service response: 109ms

(RDS slow query log for the same time window shows a full table scan on the carts table — no index on user_id column)
tasks.diagnosis: The 8-second checkout wasn't a network issue, an application logic issue, or an external API issue — it was one specific database query doing a full table scan because the user_id column on the carts table had no index. CloudWatch metrics correctly showed average latency was fine (most queries are fast) but couldn't identify WHICH step in WHICH request was slow. X-Ray's trace pinpointed the exact span, making a 5-line analysis possible that would have taken hours of log-digging with metrics alone.
tasks.fix: Add an index on carts.user_id in the database. This is a database optimization task, not a monitoring task — but X-Ray is what made it findable in minutes rather than hours. Also add a CloudWatch alarm on p99 latency in addition to average, so future tail-latency degradations are caught proactively rather than only when a customer complains.
tasks.explanation: This X-Ray's real payoff — CloudWatch 'latency is fine on average' kaatudhu, X-Ray 'specifically this DB query in this request took 7.8 seconds because of a missing index' kaatudhu. This exact difference: aggregate vs individual request trace.

Compared against: the Week 14 real incidents had zero response; the missing-index slow checkout was hurting ~1% of users for an unknown duration before being found. The ₹24.30/month buys the ability to find problems in minutes instead of days, or not at all. This is not a cost trade-off worth debating.
